# Microbiome 101 - Very Short!

What is microbiome? This figure describes it so well though.


![](/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/microbiome.png)


One method (from many) to identify microbiome is using amplicon targeted sequencing, that target special region of DNA, such as 16s rRNA (bacteria), ITS (fungi or eukaryote) and COI (usually for fish-related). 

We can use this DNA region since it contains conserve region, means the region always exist for each organism type, but also contains the hypervariable region, means the region are changed due to organism type.


![](/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/hypervariable_region.png)


Based on these hypervariable regions, Hulpusch et al (2023) use V1-V3 regions to check the effect of dilution towards synthetic mock community. We will use the result of their research during this session, Bioinformatics Workflow using R.

# Load dataset for phyloseq

`phyloseq` is a library for microbiome workflow in R. The minimal input are **ASV/OTU table** and **taxonomy table**, and the output from these files are called as `phyloseq object`. 

```{r phyloseq-import-data}

# Load dataset

otu_file <- "/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/otu.tsv"
tax_file <- "/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/tax.tsv"
meta_file <- "/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/metadata.tsv"

otu <- read.delim(otu_file, header = TRUE, row.names = 1, sep = "\t", check.names = FALSE)
tax <- read.delim(tax_file, header = TRUE, row.names = 1, sep = "\t", check.names = FALSE)
meta <- read.delim(meta_file, header = TRUE, row.names = 1, sep = "\t", check.names = FALSE)
tax[tax == "unidentified"] <- NA

# Preparation for phyloseq file

otu <- otu_table(as.matrix(otu), taxa_are_rows = TRUE)
tax <- tax_table(as.matrix(tax))
meta <- sample_data(meta)

# Making phyloseq object

ps <- phyloseq(otu, tax, meta)
ps

# Save as RDS object. Change the address based on your working directory.

saveRDS(ps, "/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/ps.rds")
```
# Taxabar Plot

Taxabar Plot is a stacked-bar plot, contains taxa for all samples that are expressed as relative abundance (%), which is obtained from fraction of taxa divided by sum of taxa in a sample.

![](/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/taxabarplot.png)

```{r taxabarplot}

# Start here. This is taxabar plot that will show top n taxa within samples.

tax_rank <- "Genus"        # "Phylum"/"Class"/"Order"/"Family"/"Genus"/...
top_n <- 10                # keep top N taxa by mean abundance

# Load color
c17_pastel<- c("skyblue2", "#FB9A99", "palegreen2","#CAB2D6", "#FDBF6F", "khaki2",
               "maroon", "orchid1", "deeppink1", "lightblue2", "steelblue4",
               "darkturquoise", "darkorange4", "brown", "#FF7F00", "gold1","#6A3D9A")


# Set color for "Other category"
other_color <- "gray70"  

# 1) Agglomerate at chosen taxonomic rank. tax_glom() is a Phyloseq function to agglomerate taxa based on a taxonomic level
ps_rank <- tax_glom(ps, taxrank = tax_rank)

# 2) Convert to relative abundance per sample. transform_sample_counts() will convert each taxa into relative abundance based on total reads.
ps_rel <- transform_sample_counts(ps_rank, function(x) (x / sum(x)*100))

# 3) Melt to long dataframe
df <- psmelt(ps_rel)

# 4) Summarise abundance per Sample x Taxon
df_summary <- df %>%
  group_by(Sample, .data[[tax_rank]]) %>%
  summarise(Abundance = sum(Abundance), .groups = "drop")

# 5) Find TOP N taxa by mean abundance across samples
top_taxa <- df_summary %>%
  group_by(.data[[tax_rank]]) %>%
  summarise(mean_abundance = mean(Abundance), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_abundance)) %>%
  slice_head(n = top_n) %>%
  pull(.data[[tax_rank]])

# 6) Collapse everything else into "Other"
df_summary <- df_summary %>%
  mutate(
    !!tax_rank := ifelse(.data[[tax_rank]] %in% top_taxa, .data[[tax_rank]], "Other")
  ) %>%
  group_by(Sample, .data[[tax_rank]]) %>%
  summarise(Abundance = sum(Abundance), .groups = "drop")

# 7) Order taxa by mean abundance (descending) but force "Other" last
tax_order <- df_summary %>%
  group_by(.data[[tax_rank]]) %>%
  summarise(mean_abundance = mean(Abundance), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_abundance)) %>%
  pull(.data[[tax_rank]])

tax_order <- c(setdiff(tax_order, "Other"), "Other")

df_summary <- df_summary %>%
  mutate(!!tax_rank := factor(.data[[tax_rank]], levels = tax_order))

# Color map
color_map <- setNames(c(c17_pastel[1:(length(tax_order)-1)], other_color), tax_order)

ggplot(df_summary, aes(x = Sample, y = Abundance, fill = .data[[tax_rank]])) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = color_map) +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Relative Abundance (%)", fill = tax_rank)

```

# Alpha Diversity

Alpha diversity is a calculation of taxa availability (richness) and the evenness of taxa within a community. The ability to define alpha diversity is important, since based on this metrics, we are able to determine which community with diverse microbiome, or even whether the community is dominated by one or some taxa.

![](/Users/hakimbazol/Documents/03_projects/r_for_biological_data_analysis/session2/alpha_diversity.png)

## Alpha diversity calculation

```{r alpha-diversity}

# Agglomerate taxa, since alpha diversity may differ based on different taxonomic level

ps_glom_genus <- tax_glom(ps, taxrank=rank_names(ps)[6])

# Calculate alpha diversity, using pre-installed library in phyloseq

alpha <- estimate_richness(ps_glom_genus, 
                           measures = c("Observed",
                                        "Shannon"
                                        )) %>%
  dplyr::rename(Richness = Observed) 

rownames(alpha) <- gsub("\\.", "-", rownames(alpha))

# Show alpha diversity table

alpha
```

## Alpha diversity plot

Before we are going to observe the alpha diversity, there are some things that we need to do!

1. Merge the calculation result with metadata (we get if from Phyloseq object)
2. Make the data in long format using `pivot_longer()` function
3. Finally, the data is ready to plot!

Let's breakdown all the step below!

### Alpha diversity merging with metadata

```{r alpha-diversity-merging-data}

# Since the data is quite many, I subset the data up until D3. Feel free to try for more data!
# As we have category and values, the visualization that able to cover that is boxplot.

# Prepare the dataset

meta <- data.frame(sample_data(ps))

alpha_w_metadata <- merge(alpha,
                          meta,
                          by = 0)

# Subset the metadata up until D3

alpha_w_metadata_d3 <- alpha_w_metadata %>%
  filter(Dilution %in% c("D0", "D1", "D2", "D3"))

alpha_w_metadata_d3

```

### Make the data in long format using `pivot_longer()`

```{r alpha-diversity-joint}

# As we have category and values, the visualization that able to cover that is boxplot.
# Making dataset as in long format

alpha_diversity_joint <- alpha_w_metadata_d3 %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Shannon, Richness),
               names_to = "variable",
               values_to = "value")

alpha_diversity_joint

```

### `ggplot()` ready to take action!

```{r alpha-diversity-plot}

# As we have category and values, the visualization that able to cover that is boxplot.

# Define group for statistical test
group_list <- unique(alpha_w_metadata_d3$Dilution)
  
# Making comparisons that we compare in the plot
my_comparisons <- combn(group_list, 2, simplify = F)

# Plot the alpha diversity based on specific category
ggplot(alpha_diversity_joint,
       aes(x = Dilution,
           y = value,
           color = Dilution )) +
  
# Define boxplot for drawing
    geom_boxplot() +

# Define statistical test for drawing
  ggpubr::stat_compare_means(method = "t.test", label = "p.signif", 
                               comparisons = my_comparisons,
                               tip.length = 0.01,
                               label.y.npc = "0.5") +
  
# Define color set. You can browse many color that is available in R. 
# See it in https://r-graph-gallery.com/38-rcolorbrewers-palettes.html

  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +

# Making limit of y-axis
    
  ylim(0, NA) +
  
# Define theme and making no label in x and y axis
    
  theme_bw() +
  
  labs(x = "", y = "") +
  
# Separate the plot using specific column

  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y")
```
